questions.prompt: What is the correct architectural role of a QPU in nearly every real quantum application today?
options: A coprocessor called by classical code for a bounded sub-task, such as evaluating a cost function
The sole processor running the entire application end to end, with no classical code involved
A device that replaces the need for any classical control flow
A storage device for intermediate optimization results
A device that can branch on its own measurement results without classical help
A general-purpose replacement for a classical CPU
questions.explain: A QPU executes a fixed circuit and returns measurement counts; it cannot branch on results or control program flow. It is architecturally a coprocessor invoked for a bounded task, exactly like a GPU in a classical ML pipeline.
questions.distractorExplain: Options describing the QPU as running the whole program, replacing classical control flow, or branching on its own results all contradict the fact that a QPU has no control-flow capability -- those decisions must always be made by classical code.

questions.prompt: In the variational hybrid loop pattern, which single step is the only one that actually touches the QPU?
options: Executing the circuit for N shots and returning measurement counts
Initializing the parameters
The classical optimizer proposing new parameters
Checking the convergence criterion
questions.explain: Of the seven steps in the variational loop, only circuit execution runs on quantum hardware -- initialization, cost computation, the optimizer step, and convergence checking are all classical.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: using the parameter-shift rule, one iteration of optimizing a circuit with p parameters requires (2 x p) + ________ total circuit evaluations.
questions.explain: The parameter-shift rule needs 2 evaluations per parameter (shifted up and down) plus exactly 1 additional evaluation for the cost function itself, giving (2p)+1 total evaluations per iteration.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that correctly distinguishes 'quantum as a coprocessor' (Pattern A) from 'quantum as the whole program' (Pattern B).
options: Pattern A involves a classical optimizer iteratively driving circuit evaluations; Pattern B is a single circuit execution with no iterative feedback
Pattern A is the dominant pattern in production hybrid systems today
Pattern B's classic use cases (e.g., Shor's-scale factoring) require hardware scale that doesn't exist yet
Pattern B requires more classical orchestration engineering than Pattern A
Pattern A cannot be simulated on a classical computer during development
questions.explain: Pattern A's iterative classical-quantum loop (vs. Pattern B's one-shot circuit) is the structural distinction; Pattern A dominates production use today; and Pattern B's textbook algorithms need hardware scale that isn't available yet. Pattern A actually requires MORE classical orchestration effort than Pattern B, and Pattern A is specifically designed to be simulator-testable during development.

questions.prompt: A team proposes developing and debugging a 150-iteration VQE loop directly against real IonQ Aria hardware from day one. What is the main problem with this plan?
options: Running a buggy, unfinished loop repeatedly at real-hardware prices (tens of thousands of dollars for a full run) wastes money that a free classical simulator would have avoided during development
Real hardware cannot execute a VQE circuit more than once
IonQ Aria does not support variational algorithms
This plan is actually the recommended approach with no real downside
questions.explain: As shown in the variational loop lesson, a full real-hardware run of this scale can cost tens of thousands of dollars -- running a half-debugged version of it repeatedly during development is the exact mistake a simulator-first workflow avoids.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before a classical feature vector can be loaded as quantum state amplitudes, it must be ________ so that the sum of its squared entries equals exactly 1.
questions.explain: A valid quantum state's amplitudes must satisfy the unit-norm constraint (squared magnitudes summing to 1). Normalization is the mandatory classical preprocessing step that enforces this before amplitude encoding.

questions.prompt: Select every TRUE statement about amplitude encoding versus angle encoding.
options: Amplitude encoding needs log2(n) qubits for n features; angle encoding needs n qubits
Amplitude encoding mandatorily requires unit-norm normalization; angle encoding does not have this hard constraint
Angle encoding typically produces a shallower circuit than amplitude encoding for an arbitrary vector
Both encodings require exactly the same number of qubits for any feature count
Angle encoding becomes impractical at large feature counts because it needs one qubit per feature
questions.explain: Amplitude encoding's logarithmic qubit scaling and mandatory normalization, angle encoding's shallower circuits, and angle encoding's linear (impractical at scale) qubit requirement are all correct per the data-preparation lesson. The two encodings do NOT require the same qubit count for a given feature count -- that's the whole tradeoff.

questions.prompt: For a 20-parameter circuit optimized over 100 iterations, why can SPSA end up far cheaper in total QPU cost than the parameter-shift rule, even though SPSA needs more iterations to converge to the same accuracy?
options: SPSA's per-iteration cost (2 evaluations, regardless of parameter count) is so much lower than parameter-shift's per-parameter scaling (2p+1) that even a 3x iteration penalty still leaves SPSA cheaper overall
SPSA does not use any quantum hardware at all
SPSA always converges in fewer iterations than parameter-shift, with no exceptions
Parameter-shift always costs less than SPSA for any circuit size
questions.explain: The lesson's worked example shows parameter-shift costing roughly 20x more than SPSA for 100 iterations on a 20-parameter circuit; even after accounting for SPSA needing several times more iterations, its far lower per-iteration cost keeps it cheaper overall -- the crossover point the lesson describes.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that correctly describes post-processing of quantum measurement results.
options: A quantum backend returns a dictionary of bitstring counts, not a final computed answer
An expectation value should always be reported together with its standard error
When combining results from multiple circuit submissions with different shot counts, each should be weighted by its own shot count, not simply averaged
A sign/basis convention error in post-processing code typically causes the backend to throw a visible error
Readout-error mitigation, where used, is applied as a classical correction step to raw counts
questions.explain: Raw counts, mandatory standard-error reporting, shot-weighted aggregation, and classical readout-error correction are all correct per the post-processing lesson. A sign/basis error does NOT throw a visible error -- it silently flips results, which is exactly why it's dangerous.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: splitting a pipeline into normalize(), submit_and_wait(), and aggregate() lets the pre- and post-processing logic be tested as ________ functions, with no network dependency and zero QPU cost.
questions.explain: normalize() and aggregate() are pure functions -- no side effects, no I/O -- so they can be unit-tested with hardcoded inputs instantly and for free, unlike submit_and_wait(), which needs a real integration test.

questions.prompt: Why do all major cloud quantum provider APIs use an asynchronous submit-then-poll job lifecycle instead of a blocking call-and-return model?
options: A QPU job can sit in a queue for seconds to hours depending on device demand, so there is no way to 'call and block' the way you would for a local simulator
Asynchronous APIs are required by government regulation
Quantum circuits take too long to execute once they reach the device
Polling is simply a stylistic preference with no technical reason behind it
questions.explain: Because queue wait is highly variable and can be very long, every major provider exposes an async submit/poll (or subscribe) lifecycle rather than a blocking call, so orchestration code must be built around this from the start.

questions.prompt: Select every TRUE statement about orchestrating a hybrid pipeline's latency, based on the measured stage-timing breakdown (queue wait ~99% of total).
options: Reducing the 40ms QPU execution time would have almost no effect on total iteration latency
Batching multiple circuit evaluations into one program-set submission reduces how many times queue wait is paid, not the queue wait itself
A naive unbatched submission of 17 evaluations per iteration pays 17 separate queue waits
Optimizing the classical pre/post-processing code is the highest-leverage latency improvement available
Batching can produce roughly a 16-17x wall-clock speedup per iteration in the lesson's worked example
questions.explain: Since queue wait dominates at ~99% of total time, execution-time optimization is nearly irrelevant, batching reduces how often queue wait is paid (not its duration), unbatched submissions pay queue wait per evaluation, and the lesson's batching example shows roughly a 16.8x speedup. Classical pre/post-processing is a tiny fraction of total time, so optimizing it is NOT the highest-leverage option.

questions.prompt: A quantum cloud job fails because the device it was queued for went offline for recalibration mid-queue. According to the error-handling decision table, what is the correct response?
options: Retry, but route the retry to a different available device rather than the same offline one
Never retry this job under any circumstances
Retry on the exact same device repeatedly until it comes back online
Immediately fail the entire multi-iteration optimization run
Silently substitute a zero value for this evaluation and continue
Delete the job record so the failure is not logged
questions.explain: Device-offline failures are retryable, but retrying the same offline device wastes time -- the correct response routes the retry to an alternate available device, as specified in the error-handling decision table.
questions.distractorExplain: Retrying the same offline device, never retrying, failing the whole run, silently substituting a value, or deleting the record all violate the lesson's explicit guidance to retry on a DIFFERENT device while keeping the failure visible in logs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: with a base delay of 500ms, exponential backoff computes each retry's delay cap as 500 times 2 raised to the power of the ________ number (0-indexed).
questions.explain: The formula is min(cap, base x 2^attempt) -- the delay cap grows exponentially with the 0-indexed attempt number, which is what desynchronizes retries over time and reduces load on a congested system.

questions.prompt: Select every fallback option the lesson lists, in the order of preference it recommends, once retries are exhausted for a failed quantum job.
options: Retry on a different, available device
Fall back to a classical simulator for that one evaluation, clearly flagged as lower-fidelity
Explicitly fail the iteration and let the calling optimizer handle the missing data point
Silently substitute a zero value with no flag
Permanently shut down the entire orchestration service
questions.explain: The lesson's preferred fallback order is: try a different device first, then a flagged simulator substitute, then an explicit failure -- never a silent substitution or a full service shutdown, both of which violate the lesson's guidance against silent corruption.

questions.prompt: For a 200-task, 1,000-shot-per-task job, approximately how much more does running it on IonQ Aria ($0.30/task + $0.03/shot) cost compared to Rigetti Ankaa-3 ($0.30/task + $0.0009/shot)?
options: About 2x more
Exactly the same cost on both devices
Rigetti Ankaa-3 is actually more expensive in this scenario
questions.explain: IonQ Aria: 200x$0.30 + 200,000x$0.03 = $6,060.00. Rigetti Ankaa-3: 200x$0.30 + 200,000x$0.0009 = $240.00. The per-shot fee difference drives a roughly 25x total cost gap for the identical workload.

questions.prompt: Select every TRUE statement about AWS Braket 'program sets' as a cost-reduction mechanism.
options: Program sets let multiple circuits share a single per-task fee instead of paying it once per circuit
The per-shot cost is unaffected by using program sets -- the saving comes entirely from the per-task fee
In the lesson's verified example, 100 circuits at 1,000 shots each dropped from $120.00 to $90.30 using program sets
Program sets eliminate the per-shot fee entirely
Program sets also reduce how many times queue wait is paid, which is a latency benefit as well as a cost benefit
questions.explain: Program sets amortize the per-task fee across many circuits (not the per-shot fee, which is unaffected), matching the lesson's verified $120.00 -> $90.30 example, and they also reduce how many separate queue waits are paid -- a latency benefit in addition to the cost saving. They do not eliminate per-shot fees.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a measured expectation value's standard error scales as 1 over the square root of shots, meaning to halve the standard error you need ________ times as many shots.
questions.explain: Since standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(shots), halving it requires multiplying shots by 2^2=4 -- exactly the relationship shown going from 1,000 shots (stderr 0.0316) to 4,000 shots (stderr 0.0158).

questions.prompt: A team pads their shot count from 2,500 to 10,000 shots per task 'just to be safe,' even though their downstream decision only needs a standard error of about 0.02. What is the main problem with this, according to the shot-budgets lesson?
options: This padding has a direct, computable extra dollar cost for precision the use case's own decision threshold doesn't actually require
10,000 shots is technically impossible for any provider to execute
Padding shots always makes the result less accurate
There is no problem; more shots are always worth the cost regardless of the use case
questions.explain: The lesson frames shot-budget sizing as a use-case-driven decision: padding beyond the precision a downstream decision actually needs has a specific, computable cost ($1,350 extra in the lesson's example) that buys precision nobody needed.

questions.prompt: A production VQE workload is found to cost roughly 34x its allocated monthly budget. Select every lever the resource-management lab identifies as a way to reduce this cost, along with its correct effect.
options: Reducing shots per evaluation cuts cost proportionally but increases standard error only by the square root of the reduction factor
Reducing run frequency (e.g., daily to weekly) cuts monthly cost roughly in proportion to the frequency reduction
Reducing iteration count via a tighter convergence tolerance can reduce cost, as shown in the variational loop lesson's convergence example
Switching to a more expensive device always reduces total cost
Combining shot reduction and frequency reduction can multiply their individual savings factors together
questions.explain: Shot reduction (proportional cost cut, square-root precision loss), frequency reduction (roughly proportional monthly savings), tighter convergence tolerance (fewer iterations), and combining levers (multiplicative savings) are all correct per the lab. Switching to a MORE expensive device would increase, not reduce, cost.

questions.prompt: Applying the four-question scoping method to the capstone's portfolio-risk VQE project, which pattern does it fall under?
options: Pattern A (coprocessor), because a classical optimizer iteratively drives an ansatz circuit to evaluate a Hamiltonian expectation value each iteration
Pattern B (whole program), because the ground-state energy is computed from one single circuit execution
Neither pattern, since ground-state energy estimation isn't a quantum-shaped problem
Pattern B, because this problem requires fault-tolerant qubits that don't exist yet
questions.explain: The capstone's variational structure -- a classical optimizer driving iterative circuit evaluations of a Hamiltonian expectation value -- is the textbook Pattern A case, buildable on current NISQ hardware for a small molecular system.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: for the capstone's 6-parameter ansatz using the parameter-shift rule, one iteration requires (6 x 2) + 1 = ________ circuit evaluations.
questions.explain: Following the parameter-shift formula (2 x params + 1), a 6-parameter ansatz needs (6x2)+1 = 13 evaluations per iteration, the number used throughout the capstone's budgeting and orchestration design.

questions.prompt: Select every TRUE statement about the capstone project's success criteria, as defined at kickoff.
options: Success criteria focus on classical engineering quality: orchestration correctness, cost/latency tracking, reported standard error, and log traceability
The orchestration layer must correctly handle at least one simulated failure/retry scenario
A reviewer should be able to read the operational log after a run and answer what it cost and whether anything failed, without re-running anything
Success explicitly requires the quantum result to outperform a classical baseline
The project's success criteria were deliberately designed to not depend on achieving quantum advantage
questions.explain: The kickoff lesson explicitly frames success around engineering quality (orchestration, tracking, standard error, log traceability) and deliberately avoids requiring quantum advantage, since that's often not achievable with current hardware -- the opposite of option 4's claim.

questions.prompt: The capstone's project brief flagged that running the workload daily would cost roughly $21,120/month, but the one-run capstone demo only cost $960. What does the final architecture-review lesson say about this discrepancy?
options: A genuine review must revisit this flagged-but-unresolved cost projection rather than letting it quietly disappear just because a single demo run succeeded
The discrepancy is irrelevant since the capstone only needed to demonstrate one successful run
The $21,120/month figure was a calculation error that should be ignored
Monthly cost projections don't need to be part of an architecture review
questions.explain: The wrap-up lesson explicitly treats this unresolved flag as an 'open item' that a real sign-off review must surface and recommend following up on, rather than letting a single successful demo run make the earlier business-cost concern seem resolved.

questions.prompt: Select every TRUE statement about how the capstone's architecture generalizes beyond VQE, according to the wrap-up lesson.
options: The state machine, batching strategy, retry/fallback decision table, and cost ledger/circuit-breaker all carry over unchanged to other Pattern A algorithms like QAOA or variational classifiers
Swapping the ansatz and cost function is the main algorithm-specific change needed to apply this architecture elsewhere
The simulator-first testing discipline is VQE-specific and does not apply to other variational algorithms
This reusable orchestration pattern, not a working VQE demo, is described as the actual deliverable of the course
The backend adapter abstraction from Chapter 3 is part of what makes this architecture swappable between providers
questions.explain: The classical orchestration pattern (state machine, batching, retry/fallback, cost tracking, and the provider-abstraction layer) is explicitly framed as algorithm-agnostic and transferable, with the ansatz/cost function being the main thing that changes. Simulator-first testing is explicitly NOT VQE-specific -- it applies to any variational algorithm.

questions.prompt: A ticket proposes using Grover's algorithm to search 10 million records in production next quarter, with no classical optimizer loop. Why does the architecture-patterns lab classify this as not buildable on current hardware?
options: The required qubit count (~24) and the roughly 3,162 oracle/diffusion repetitions needed exceed what current NISQ hardware can execute reliably
Grover's algorithm has never been implemented on any quantum hardware
Search problems can never be formulated as quantum circuits
The ticket is a Pattern A problem that was incorrectly scoped as Pattern B
questions.explain: The lab's four-question method correctly identifies this as Pattern B (one-shot search, no classical loop) but flags that the required qubit count and repetition count for real reliability exceed current NISQ hardware capability -- an honest 'not buildable at this scale' answer, not a miscategorization.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: for the vector [2,2,2,2], the norm is sqrt(2^2+2^2+2^2+2^2) = sqrt(16) = ________, giving a normalized vector of [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5].
questions.explain: Sum of squares = 4x(2^2) = 16, and sqrt(16) = 4. Dividing each entry by 4 gives [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5], whose squared entries sum to exactly 1.0 as required for valid amplitude encoding.

questions.prompt: Select every TRUE statement about cloud quantum provider API differences covered in the provider-overview lesson.
options: AWS Braket bills primarily via a per-task fee plus a per-shot fee that varies by device
IBM Quantum's Pay-As-You-Go plan bills primarily by wall-clock runtime seconds
A single 'cost = shots x price_per_shot' formula works correctly for estimating cost on every provider
Checking device/backend status metadata before submission is a zero-cost way to avoid submitting to an offline or badly-queued device
The provider-abstraction layer's estimate_cost() method must account for which pricing dimension a given provider actually bills on
questions.explain: Braket's per-task+per-shot billing, IBM's runtime-second billing, the value of pre-submission metadata checks, and the abstraction layer's need to handle different pricing dimensions are all correct. A single shots-based formula does NOT work across all providers, since IBM bills by runtime seconds, not shots.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say IBM Quantum's cost can't be estimated the same way as AWS Braket's, even for the same circuit and shot count?
options: IBM bills by wall-clock runtime seconds, which depends on circuit depth and queueing behavior rather than shot count directly, unlike Braket's shots-and-tasks-based pricing
IBM Quantum does not charge for any usage at all
AWS Braket and IBM Quantum actually use identical billing formulas
IBM only accepts circuits with a fixed, pre-set shot count of exactly 1,000
questions.explain: IBM's Pay-As-You-Go pricing is based on billable runtime seconds, a fundamentally different dimension from Braket's per-task-plus-per-shot model, which is exactly why a single shared cost formula can't be used across both providers.

questions.prompt: Select every TRUE statement about the capstone project's error-handling and cost-tracking implementation (Lesson 21).
options: A failed-then-retried submission is logged as two separate ledger entries, making the wasted spend from the failure visible
The cost circuit-breaker checks cumulative cost after every submission, not just at the end of the run
A circuit validation failure triggers the same retry-with-backoff process as a device-offline failure
Fault injection is used to deterministically test error-handling paths without waiting for a real device failure
The circuit-breaker ceiling was set with 25% headroom above the originally planned $960 budget
questions.explain: Visible wasted-spend logging, per-submission circuit-breaker checks, fault-injection testing, and the $1,200 ceiling (25% headroom over $960) are all correct per the project lesson. A circuit validation failure does NOT retry -- it's logged as a code bug, unlike a device-offline failure, which does retry with backoff.
